context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
4. Late Holocene sea level indicators
4.1 Geomorphological indicators
4.1.1 Marine notches
Submerged marine tidal notches have been found on the NW coast of Paros, at Aspra Chomata near Ampelas
village, and on the SW cliff of Gaidouronisi, a rocky islet a short distance off the NE coast of Paros (Figure 1c).
Two marine notches were cut into the sandstones of the molassic bedrock on Aspra Chomata coast, today both
submerged. The deepest notch has an opening of 1 m, inward depth 1.10 m and a base at 2.15 m to 2.20 m bmsl. The
shallowest notch has an opening of 0.30 m, inward depth 0.45 m and a base at 0.55 m to 0.60 m bmsl (Figure 2a).
Two submerged marine notches are also observed along the SW carbonate cliff of Gaidouronisi Islet. The base
of the deepest notch is at 2.10 m to 2.13 m bmsl, has an opening of 0.59 m to 0.90 m and inward depth 0.33 to 0.53
m. The shallowest notch has an opening of 0.30 m to 0.59 m, inward depth 0.19 m to 0.53 m and a base at 0.37 m to
0.55 m bmsl (Figure 2b).
In summary, two marine tidal notches were identified along the rocky coast of Paros: the base of the deepest
notch is at an average depth of 2.15 ± 0.05 and of the shallowest at 0.45 ± 0.10 m bmsl (Figure 4a).

context_leads.title: New insights on the relative sea level changes during the Late Holocene along the coast of Paros Island and the northern Cyclades (Greece)
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
4.1.2 Beachrocks
The systematic measurement and mapping of beachrocks at four locations along the coast of Paros (Figure 1c)
enabled us to define five distinct beachrock generations (Ι, ΙΙ, ΙΙΙ, IV and V) that were formed during five different sea
level stands. Three distinct beachrock generations were also identified at a fifth location (Tsoukalia) on the eastern
coast of Paros (Figure 1c). Since the beachrocks are highy fragmented, poorly preserved and shifted from their original
position, their depths are not representative and therefore were not taken into consideration.
The earliest beachrock generation (Ι) was found in Logaras Bay at 4.90 ± 0.10 m bmsl. It is a slab 113 m long, 20 m
wide and 0.85 m thick (Figures 2c, 3b). The next beachrock generation (II) was found in the bays of Logaras and Molos
and on the Martselo coast at 3.50 ± 0.20 m bmsl. The length of the beachrock slabs varies between 108 m and 262 m,
with a width of between 17 m and 30 m and thickness between 0.30 m and 1.50 m (Figures 3a, b, c). The subsequent
beachrock generation (III) develops along the Martselo coast for a total length of 100 m, with a width of 8 m and a
thickness of 0.65 m. Its seaward base was measured at 2.55 ± 0.15 m bmsl (Figure 3c). The following beachrock
generation (IV) was found in the bays of Logaras and Molos and on the Martselo coast at 1.35 ± 0.20 m bmsl. The
length of the beachrock slabs varies between 130 m and 203 m, with a width of between 14 m and 30 m and thickness
between 0.20 m and 0.60 m (Figures 2d, 3a, b, c). The most recent beachrock generation (V) was found on the coast of
Pounda at 0.80 ± 0.10 m bmsl. It has a length of 42 m, with a width of 3.50 m and thickness of 0.30 m (Figure 3d).
The cements of the beachrocks of Paros reflect diagenesis within the intertidal environment. Microscopic studies
of thin sections of samples from the submerged beachrocks [Karkani et al., 2017] revealed well-rounded grains,
bioclasts (forams and gastropods) and early intertidal cement between grains. The early intertidal cements were
mainly characterised by isopachous radiaxial ﬁbrous high magnesian calcite (HMC) crystals or small bladed isopachous
fringe of limpid and contiguous HMC crystals. Evidence of micritic ﬁlling including internal sediments and peloidal
cement was also observed, generally following a ﬁrst fringe of early intertidal cement [Karkani et al., 2017].
Data on each beachrock generation surveyed along the coast of Paros Island are presented in Table 1 and plans
of the submerged beachrocks are shown in Figure 3. In Figure 4a, the average depths of the base of the seaward end
of each beachrock generation and the base of tidal notches for each survey location are shown. Error bars refer to
the uncertainties in depths as estimated from multiple measurements at the same geomorphological feature.

4.2 Archaeological indicators
4.2.1 The Late Neolithic settlement of Saliagos
The Neolithic settlement of Saliagos lies on the western part of the Saliagos Islet. The rocky islet is located at
the northern end of the Paros-Antiparos Strait and is the intermediate of three small islands that almost form a
straight line: Magrines Island ~400 m to the north, and Revmatonisi ~200 m to the south (Figure 1c). Saliagos
covers an area of 8,000 m2, rises to a height of less than 5 m above the present sea level and, on its NW side, is
bordered by a 3 m-high sheer cliff falling to the sea. The depth of the rocky seabed between Saliagos and
Revmatonisi, and that in the Paros-Antiparos Strait, just to the south of Revmatonisi, does not exceed 5 m (Figures
1c, 5a). There is no source of fresh water on Saliagos [Morrison, 1968], but there is an undersea fresh-water spring
off the west side of Revmatonisi whose location would then have been above sea level [Evans and Renfrew, 1968].
It is remarkable that there is almost no soil-cover left on the three islands, the exception being the southern part
of Saliagos where soil is preserved to a depth sometimes exceeding 2 m [Evans and Renfrew, 1968].
The study of the pottery and other small finds places the Saliagos culture in the transition from Middle to Late
Neolithic in mainland Greece, within the range of 4300 BC to 3700 BC [Zafeiropoulos, 1960; Evans and Renfrew,
1968]. Five radiocarbon datings (one of soil rich in organic matter and four from shells of the large bivalve Spondylus
gaederopus) fall within this time range (4408 ± 76 BC ÷ 3766 ± 85 BC) [Evans and Renfrew, 1968]. The sequence of
dates is in conformity with the Saliagos stratigraphy, as revealed by the archaeological excavations [Evans and
Renfrew, 1968].
No evidence of burials has been found in Saliagos and it is very possible that some sort of cemetery, perhaps on
the slopes of the promontory, has been destroyed or submerged [Evans and Renfrew, 1968]. Abundant remains of
sheep, goats, cattle and pigs show clearly that mixed farming consituted the basis of life here, while no convincing
evidence of hunting has been found. Large quantities of fishbones, mainly of tunny and shellfish but even a cuttlefish
guard, offered a remarkable insight into the diet of the prehistoric islanders. No fish-hooks have been found in
Saliagos. The shallow and narrow configuration of the bays at Saliagos may have been favourable for fishing by
driving fish ashore with nets and boats and then spearing them with obsidian points [Evans and Renfrew, 1968].

RSL change on Paros, N Cyclades
An important ancient technical work is the submerged elongate rockfill, located about 800 m south of the
northern insular complex of Paros-Antiparos Strait and 200 m south of the pier of Antiparos. Starting at a distance
of 37 m off the contemporary coast is directed NNW-SSE towards the coast of Paros (Figure 5a). The rockfill has a
total length of about 700 m and appears to be continouous for some 250 m from its beginning on Antiparos coast,
while for about 450 m towards Paros is distinguished in parts. It has a width of 3-4 m and a maximum height of 2
m. It’s top and base are at a maximum depth of 3 m and 5.20 m bmsl, respectively (Figure 5a).
The extensive farming and craft activity at Saliagos during its short occupation of 200 to 400 years, as the
archaeological survey has revealed [Evans and Renfrew, 1968], could not be limited to such a small islet, lacking
planation, fresh water and vegetation. A wider area to the south, as the bathymetry of the northern part of ParosAntiparos Strait implies, which included Revmatonisi to the south and was joined to the coast of the two islands
on either side, forming a “transit corridor”, could justify the establishment and development of the Late Neolithic
settlement (Figure 5b). According to the palaeogeographic reconstruction of the coast (Figure 5b), the ancient
rockfill, today submerged, was placed at the southernmost edge of the then land.

4.2.2 The Geometric breakwater of Agios Ioannis Detis
At the NW end of Naoussa Gulf, on the hill west of the Monastery of Agios Ioannis Detis (Figure 1c), rectangular
buildings of the Geometric period (8th c. BC) have been revealed [Kourayos, 2015]. A rubble mound breakwater,
today submerged, begins at the sharp seaward edge of the rocky hill (Figure 6). This has also been reported by
Papathanassopoulos and Schilardi [1981]. The breakwater develops in an E-W direction for a length of 78.50 m and
its width reaches 14 m. It consists of stones ranging from 0.20 m to 0.60 m in size. Its top surface has a width of 4
m in the western part and widens in the eastern part, reaching 9 m. The surface of the breakwater in the western
section is from 1.20 m to 1.35 m bmsl while the eastern section gradually sinks from 1.65 m to 2.35 m bmsl at its
seaward end. The depth of the sea bottom at the base of the breakwater increases from west (2.68 m) to east (6.05
m). In the central part of the breakwater, a hollow was observed, the bottom of which is at 2.60 m bmsl. It occupies
an area of 11 m2 and has an internal depth of about 1 m (Figure 6). It probably served for accumulating fuel to light
a fire to signal the position of the breakwater and hence the settlement.

4.2.3 Lighthouses, paved road, tombs and piles of stones of the Geometric or Archaic period in Zoodochos Pigi Bay
Oikonomou Island (“Nisi Oikonomou”), in truth an islet, is located at the eastern end of Naoussa Gulf (Figure
1c) and is connected to the coast of Paros opposite through a narrow sandy strip of land, forming two small bays on
both north and south sides of the strip (Figure 8a). On the SE part of Oikonomou Island, a fortified settlement,
probably dated to the Geometric and Archaic period, is preserved up to the level of its foundations [Schilardi, 1973;
Kourayos, 2015] (Figures 7, 8a). In the north bay (Zoodochos Pigi Bay) the depths do not exceed 3 m, the seabed is
sandy and an elongate reef of a maximum elevation of 0.50 m protrudes from the sea bottom only on its west side.
The reef, 250 m long and 25 m wide, is located within a distance of 100 m from the NE coast of Oikonomou Island
and follows its configuration. Two large cairn-like piles of stones lay on the reef within 42 m of each other. They have
also been reported by Fotiou [1973], who interpreted them as maritime structures. The southern pile of stones, 1.40
m high and 280 m3 in volume, has an ellipsoidal base occupying an area of 290 m2. The sea bottom on its western
side is at 2.55 m bmsl and on its eastern and southern sides between 3.10 m and 3.20 m bmsl. Its top surface, of an
area of 105 m2, is from 1.20 m to 1.80 m bmsl. In the NW part, a hollow of an area of 14 m2 and internal depth 0.40
m is observed, with its bottom at 1.60 m bmsl. The northern pile of stones, 1.70 m high and 370 m3 in volume, has
an elongate oval base occupying an area of 350 m2 at the depth of 2.90 m bmsl. Its top surface, covering an area of
140 m2, is at 1.30 m to 1.40 m bmsl. A 17 m2 hollow with internal depth of 0.20 m is also observed on the northern
side of the top surface, with its bottom at 1.40 m bmsl. The two large piles of stones were probably lighthouses,
signaling the NE coast of Oikonomou Island, with the hollows in their surface serving to accumulate fuel for lighting
fires to signal the position of the shoreline. Between the two piles of stones, rectangular carvings, most likely graves,
were observed at 3 m bmsl. Another rectangular carving – also likely to have been a grave – was found at 3.25 m bmsl
between the reef and the opposite coast, where the small church of Zoodochos Pigi is situated (Figures 7, 8a).

4.2.3 Lighthouses, paved road, tombs and piles of stones of the Geometric or Archaic period in Zoodochos Pigi Bay
Oikonomou Island (“Nisi Oikonomou”), in truth an islet, is located at the eastern end of Naoussa Gulf (Figure
1c) and is connected to the coast of Paros opposite through a narrow sandy strip of land, forming two small bays on
both north and south sides of the strip (Figure 8a). On the SE part of Oikonomou Island, a fortified settlement,
probably dated to the Geometric and Archaic period, is preserved up to the level of its foundations [Schilardi, 1973;
Kourayos, 2015] (Figures 7, 8a). In the north bay (Zoodochos Pigi Bay) the depths do not exceed 3 m, the seabed is
sandy and an elongate reef of a maximum elevation of 0.50 m protrudes from the sea bottom only on its west side.
The reef, 250 m long and 25 m wide, is located within a distance of 100 m from the NE coast of Oikonomou Island
and follows its configuration. Two large cairn-like piles of stones lay on the reef within 42 m of each other. They have
also been reported by Fotiou [1973], who interpreted them as maritime structures. The southern pile of stones, 1.40
m high and 280 m3 in volume, has an ellipsoidal base occupying an area of 290 m2. The sea bottom on its western
side is at 2.55 m bmsl and on its eastern and southern sides between 3.10 m and 3.20 m bmsl. Its top surface, of an
area of 105 m2, is from 1.20 m to 1.80 m bmsl. In the NW part, a hollow of an area of 14 m2 and internal depth 0.40
m is observed, with its bottom at 1.60 m bmsl. The northern pile of stones, 1.70 m high and 370 m3 in volume, has
an elongate oval base occupying an area of 350 m2 at the depth of 2.90 m bmsl. Its top surface, covering an area of
140 m2, is at 1.30 m to 1.40 m bmsl. A 17 m2 hollow with internal depth of 0.20 m is also observed on the northern
side of the top surface, with its bottom at 1.40 m bmsl. The two large piles of stones were probably lighthouses,

4.2.4 Ancient rock-cut trenches
Extensive series of elongate rock-cut trenches and parallel rows of rectangular cuttings have been identified at
25 locations on and off the coast of Paros, Revmatonisi, Diplo, Antiparos and Despotiko (Figure 1c). The rock-cut
trenches of Paros were first reported by Graves [1842] and Rubensohn (1901) and those on the eastern coast of
Antiparos and on Revmatonisi by Evans and Renfrew [1968] and Morrison [1968]. Fotiou [1973] has described the
cuttings found in Naoussa Gulf and Draganits (2009) as well as those on the northern coast of Despotiko. The
cuttings in Filizi Bay and the Santa Maria area, Naoussa Gulf, Zoodochos Pigi and Lageri Bays, the areas of Pounda,
Kampos, Agios Nikolaos and Voutakos in the Paros-Antiparos Strait and in the bay of Despotiko were surveyed by
the Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities in 2001 [Kraounaki, 2012].
Most of the rock-cut trenches are located on the NE side of Paros, on the eastern coast of Naoussa Gulf (8
locations) and in Santa Maria Bay (2 locations) and Filizi Bay (3 locations). Others can be found on the northern part
of the Paros-Antiparos Strait on the coast of both islands (3 locations on the SW coast of Paros and 2 locations on
the eastern coast of Antiparos), between them on the coast of Revmatonisi Island (3 locations), and to the north of
Antiparos on the coast of Diplo Island (2 locations). On the eastern coast of Paros, in Drios, only one group of
elongate cuttings was identified. Additionally, on the NE coast of Despotiko Island, there is a system of rock-cut
parallel trenches (Figure 1c).
The trenches were usually cut parallel to each other at a distance of 1 m to 8 m, with a length ranging from 13
m to 140 m and a width of 1 m to 2 m. Their orientation is mainly NE-SW (17 locations) but also NW-SE (8 locations,
either parallely (22 locations) or transversally (3 locations) with reference to the palaeoshoreline. The rectangular
cuttings, measuring 1.50 m x 1 m, have been identified at 4 locations, either in one row (2 locations) or in two to
three parallel rows (2 locations) within 3 m to 4.50 m of each other. In some cases (3 locations), rectangular cuttings
in rows were observed between the rock-cut trenches. Most of the trenches have been carved into the hard, 2 mthick, reddish, calcitic-clayey crust of the molassic clastic sequence of Paros.
There is still speculation among researchers about the use and the dating of these impressive rock-cut
constructions. From the 19th c. onward, several views have been expressed on their use. Graves [1842], who first
produced a bythometric map of the central Cyclades, and Rubensohn [1901] suggested that the trenches served as
salt-pans. Evans and Renfrew [1968] and Morrison [1968] assumed that they represent a Hellenistic field-system of
vine trenches for systematic viticulture. Fotiou [1973] interpreted the cuttings in Naoussa Gulf as harbour
installations and shipsheds. Berranger-Auserve [1992] suggested that the cuttings in Santa Maria were shipyards and
boat installations for marble export, because the ancient roads that start from the quarries end up at the coast there.
Auffray [2002], after presenting several hypotheses for the use of trenches – as grape presses for must making, or
seawater tanks for immersing wine amphorae to accelerate wine ageing, or quarries, or even shipyards – finally
adopted the last interpretation, despite the horizontal position of the trench floor. Kraounaki [2012] suggested that,
apart from shipyards and harbour installations, all other interpretations should have been considered: buildings
related to naval installations, transport systems for heavy materials (e.g. marble, wood, statues, architectural
members), fish-tanks or salt-pans, viticulture systems or even rainwater drainage systems.

Eleni Kolaiti and Nikos Mourtzas
The proposed interpretation that the rock-cut trenches were used in antiquity for systematic viticulture would
appear to be the most plausible. The natural environment of Paros favoured, and still favours, the cultivation of vine.
The technique of planting vines by digging trenches in soil or cutting them in rock during antiquity is mentioned
by ancient writers, e.g. Pliny, Strabo, Theophrastus, Xenophon, Palladius, Palladius (II.10.1), Columella (De re
Rustica, III, 13) and is reported by findings from archaeological excavations [e.g. Amouretti, 1988, 1992; Karali and
Mavrides, 1998; Lilimpaki-Akamati, 1998; Brun, 2003; Scarlatidou, 2004; Vordos, 2005]. The depth of trenches would
have been 0.70 m and a path – 3 m to 5.50 m wide - would have been left between them to allow carriages to pass.
Concerning the orientation of the vineyard, Columella (De re Rustica, III, 12, 5-6) suggested that, in very hot areas
such as Egypt, it is advisable for them to be oriented only to the north. On coastal vineyards, the favourable effect
of the sea is due to the high thermal inertia of seawater, i.e. its capacity for heat storage. Therefore, the vineyard’s
proximity to the sea blunts the daytime temperature peaks, thus creating gentler mesoclimate conditions than
those of continental areas located at the same geographical latitude and altitude. On the other hand, the constant
fresh and humid sea breeze blowing through coastal terroirs during the hot hours of the day mitigates the ambient
temperature and improves lighting conditions, thus serving the gentle ripening of grapes [Coastal-terroirs].
Evans and Renfrew [1968] and Morrison [1968] dated the trenches to the Hellenistic period. Specifically for the
area of Voutakos, the Hellenistic dating could be related to the concentration of Classical/Hellenistic ceramics found
north and west of the church of Agios Georgios [Vionis, 2006]. Auffray [2002] associated them with activities of the
Geometric period around Oikonomou Island. Kraounaki [2012], points out that their dating – in the absence of
ceramics or evidence of any type of masonry – remains problematic, and hence their use may or may not be
simultaneous, thus implying that they might belong to different periods.
With the exception of three locations, where the rock-cut trenches today are on land, they are all submerged from
the contemporary coastline up to a depth of 2.50 m. Most of them are of considerable length and found on the WSW
side of Paros, on the coast of Voutakos, Agios Nikolaos and Kampos (Figures 1c, 9a).
Three groups of trenches were found on the coast of Kampos (Figure 9b). The southernmost group, some 50 m
to the north of the small fishing port of Kampos, consists of 8 parallel trenches 3 m to 3.50 m apart, 30 m long and
3m wide each, located between the depths of 0.95 m and 1.35 m bmsl. At a distance of 200 m to the north, the second
group, consisting of 17 parallel trenches, stretches for 135 m in a NNE-SSW direction from the contemporary
coastline to 90 m offshore at the depth of 2.20 m bmsl. They are 1 m to 2.50 m wide and have an internal depth of
0.50 m. At the south end of this group of trenches, the ruins of a large building were identified, occupying an area
of 1500 m2, with abundant potsherds on its floor mixed with the collapsed masonry. The building probably served
craft and storage needs associated with the use of the rock-cut trenches. It was most likely a warehouse, where large
pithoi were placed for wine fermentation and storage [e.g. Nikolantonakis and Amoiridou, 2011]. The last and
deepest visible trace of the building is at 2.40 m bmsl, while to the northwest a large number of rectangular cuttings
with a slab cover on the top, probably graves, measuring about 1.50 m x 0.70 m each, were tracked up to a depth of
2.75 m. The third group is located some 30 m further north and consists of at least 11 trenches (Figure 9b).
At a distance of about 300 m to the south of Kampos, on the south coast of the promontory where the chapel of
Agios Nikolaos is situated (Figure 9c), a group of 20 parallel trenches 1 m to 3 m apart was found. They stretch in a
NNW-SSE direction, with a length ranging from 27 m to 70 m, a width of 1.50 m and an internal depth of 0.50 m,
with their floor dipping 1° southward. In the southern part, they reach a depth of 2.20 m bmsl. Some 20 m west of
these, there is a group of crossed trenches, with their deepest trace at 2.48 m bmsl.

corridor 1.50 m wide. The most impressive finding is a preserved marble frame with ceramic conduits, part of the
tank’s drainage system. The walls have a thickness of 0.40 m to 1.30 m and in large parts of the building stand up
to 0.30 m in height. They are built of rough stones, ceramic tiles and bricks, bound with mortar. It shows the same
typology as those of other residences, workshops or farmhouses found on Paros [e.g. Floga site, Kourayos, 2015]
that date back to the Roman period (146 BC – 4th c. AD).
The building complex is now completely submerged, with sections of the paved floor at 1.20 m bmsl and external
masonry at 1.60 m. The last trace of paving and foundations was identified 65 m offshore at 1.75 m bmsl and either
belongs to the building or is a remnant of the road that passed in front of it (Figure 10). Furthermore, the positioning
of the building with respect to the palaeoshoreline (Figure 10) implies that here may have been the coastal section
of the Roman road, which started from the Ekatontapyliani area, passing through the Roman cemetery
[Zafeiropoulou, 1998; Kourayos, 2015] and ending in the workshops area (called “Magazakia”), to which the building
complex most likely belongs.
Two large piles of stones, of circular base about 6 m in diameter, were found submerged on the seafloor some
30 m SW of the building complex. They were constructed along the shoreline on the exposed seafront of the
workshops either to protect it against the waves (protective rockfills) or to signal the then shoreline (cairn-like
landmark). Whatever the case, their current position defines the coastline of the period in which they were
constructed [Kolaiti, 2019]. The seaward base of the northern pile of stones is at 2.35 m bmsl and its top at 1.70 m
bmsl (Figure 10).

4.2.6 Roman breakwater on Krotiri coast
The ancient rubble mound breakwater on Krotiri coast, on the NW side of Paroikia Gulf (Figure 1c), was first
shown in the map made by Roux [1804], in which a depth of 6 ft (~1.83 m) is also noted just to the west of the
breakwater. The ancient breakwater was later reported by Schilardi [1981] and Papathanassopoulos and Schilardi
[1981]. Much later, Evelpidou et al. [2018], ignoring Roux’s map [1804], doubted whether the mole was ancient and
reiterated the speculations of “the locals that the breakwater is a work of Nazis during the German occupation of the
island in World War II”.
The breakwater starts about 7 m from the sandy-gravely coast and runs SE for 102 m (Figure 11). Its maximum
breadth reaches 19 m at the base, while at the top surface this does not exceed 9 m. In the central part of the
breakwater, a hollow measuring 9 m x 3 m and approximately 1 m deep was observed. The size of the rubblestones,
carefully set forming the breakwater, ranges from 0.20 m to 0.60 m. The depth of the top of the breakwater varies
between 1.10 m and 1.35 m, with the exception of its approximately 20 m long seaward end, where it increases to
1.60 m. Correspondingly, the depth at the base of the breakwater gradually increases from 1.40 m near the coast up
to 4.10 m at its seaward end (Figure 11).

4.2.9 Threshing floor and protective rockfill
The coastal plain on the NE side of Lageri Bay (Figure 1c) was an area of intense agricultural activity in the recent
past, as evidenced by at least five threshing floors preserved to date (Figure 14). According to Vionis [2006], it seems
that during the Middle Byzantine period the settled landscape was transferred from the bay of Paroikia to that of
Naoussa in the north, whereas small peasant communities made use of the fertile land surrounding rural settlements
and the safe anchorage of bays around the island.
The easternmost out of five preserved threshing floors was founded on the surface of a rocky reef, which now
forms a small submarine promontory developing in a SW direction. It has a diameter of 8 m, a perimeter wall built
of rectangular blocks, hard floor paved with slabs, of which few are currently preserved, and in its centre three large
blocks among which a wooden pole may be placed. The preserved parts of the paved floor are submerged at 0.80 m
bmsl and the foundation of the slabs at 1 m bmsl (Figure 14). The large amount of ceramic fragments around the
submerged threshing floor, some of them glazed, indicate that the area was in use either during the Venetian
domination (1207 - 1537) or possibly later during the Ottoman rule (1537-1821).
At the southern end of the lowland, within 13 m from the shoreline, three more threshing floors were found on
land, at an elevation not exceeding 1.50 m. All along the seafront, where the farmhouse and the three threshing
floors are located, a protective rockfill has been found about 7 m offshore (Figure 14). It is 172 m long and 3 m to 3.50
m wide and is made of rubblestones up to 0.40 m in size. The seaward and landward base of the rockfill is at 0.90 m
to 1 m bmsl and its top at 0.60 m to 0.65 m bmsl.

5. Discussion
Marine transgressions that occurred throughout the Late Holocene have radically changed the palaeogeography
of the coast of Paros, by submerging below sea level the coastal landscape and the maritime and other coastal
constructions from the Late Neolithic to the present.
The deepest sea level stand (I) at 4.90 ± 0.10 m bmsl is determined by the deepest beachrock generation (I) in
Logaras Bay (Figures 4b, 15a). The dating of this sea level has been indirectly achieved taking into consideration the
prerequisites for the Neolithic settlement of Saliagos to flourish between 4300 BC and 3700 BC: the intense farming
activity on Saliagos, despite the small size of the islet and its lack of fresh water and arable land and pastures
[Morrison, 1968], goes beyond the limits of the present rocky islet and implies a broader terrestrial area associated
with it, one which today is inundated by the sea. Given that the morphology of the rocky seabed has not changed
since it sunk and the maximum depth between the two islands and at Paros-Antiparos Strait to the south does not
exceed 5 m, the use and flourishing of the Saliagos site can be associated with the sea level stand at 4.90 ± 0.10 m
bmsl found on the coast of Paros (Figure 15a). The contemporary depth (at 5 m bmsl) of the rockfill, probably placed
during the same period for defence purposes at the southern edge of the then terrestrial part of Paros-Antiparos
Strait, provides further evidence on the dating of the deepest sea level stand (I).

taking into consideration the depths of the building complex and the rock-cut tombs on the Kampos coast at 2.40
m and 2.75 m bmsl, respectively (Figure 9b), human activities could have been accomplished there with sea level
3.50 ± 0.20 m (sea level stand II) lower than at present. The hypothesis of Evans and Renfrew [1968] and Morrison
[1968] that the partially submerged system of trenches on Paros, Antiparos and Revmatonisi was cut in Hellenistic
times, which means in the period between 323 and 146 BC, but also the widespread Classical/Hellenistic ceramics
in the area of Voutakos [Vionis, 2006], allow us to suggest that the sea level stand (II) could have lasted even during
the Hellenistic period (Figuure 15a).

notch on Gaidouronisi Islet, as well as on the NW coast of Paros at a depth of 2.15 m to 2.20 m bmsl, determine a
sea level stand (III) at 2.40 ± 0.25 m bmsl during the Roman period of Paros (146 BC - 4th c. AD) (Figs. 4b, 15a). From
the last visible trace of the foundations of the Roman building complex on the Paroikia coast, found at 1.75 m bmsl,
and by adding at least 0.50 m for a stone foundation course, given that the foundation was (then) constructed on
land, we can infer that the foundation level should be at 2.25 m bmsl (Figure 10). Also, the piles of stones - either
protective rockfills or cairn-like landmarks - constructed along the then shoreline in front of the building, with
their base at 2.35 m bmsl, are linked to the sea level (III) at 2.40 ± 0.25 m found on the coast of Paros (Figure 15a).

floor at 0.30 m above high tide in order for it to be kept dry, which suggests a minimum “functional height” of 0.60

context_leads.title: New insights on the relative sea level changes during the Late Holocene along the coast of Paros Island and the northern Cyclades (Greece)
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
Eleni Kolaiti and Nikos Mourtzas
Τhe most recent sea level stand (VΙ), determined by the shallowest marine notch on Gaidouronisi Islet and at
Aspra Chomata at 0.45 ± 0.10 m (Figures 4b, 15a), is dated to the recent change in the sea level from the late 19th
c. onward. Although we have reservations about the accuracy of the depth (6 ft) given in Roux’s map [1804], a
comparison with the current average depth of the Roman breakwater on Krotiri coast roughly suggests a rsl rise of
0.45 m during the last 215 years, which matches the most recent sea level stand (VI).
Conflicting views on the rsl changes in the Cyclades have been expressed in a series of papers since 2012.
Evelpidou et al. [2012b] suggested that the rsl reached ∼-2.00 m ± 0.50 at about ∼4000 BP in the adjacent western
Naxos [Karkani et al., 2019]. In a subsequent publication, Evelpidou et al. [2014] stated that the sea level was at 2.90 m before the period 3350–4200 yr BP, ‐2.30 m around 3100 yr BP, above -1.78 ± 0.50 m around 1752 ± 40 yr BP,
at -1.00 ± 0.10 m around 941 ± 40 yr BP, -0.75 ± 0.10 m about 900 BP and -0.35 ± 0.05 m around 232 ± 35 yr BP.
Karkani et al. [2017] determined three sea level stands along the coast of Paros: the shallowest between -0.80 ± 0.20
and -1.80 ± 0.20 m yielded an age between 1500 ± 70 yr BP and 1000 ± 160 yr BP and the deepest sea level at -5.60
± 0.50 m between 1720 ± 80 yr BP and 1390 ± 190 yr BP, although the authors admitted that the latter age “does
not seem credible for such a deep shoreline”. Subsequently, Karkani et al. [2018] suggested for Paros that between
3100 and 3300 yr BP the sea level was between -1.50 m and -2.50 m. Recently, however, Karkani et al. [2019] rejected
the previous ages and stated that the rsl had risen by ∼2 m over the previous 2000 years and by at least ∼3.90 m since
∼4500 yr BP. Apart from the difficulty in following such contradictory views, the reader would have the impression
that the coastal human activities on Paros from the Late Neolithic to Modern Times had taken place underwater.
For example, if the sea level had been at -2 m to -2.50 m between 3300 yr BP [Karkani et al., 2018] and 2000 yr BP
[Karkani et al., 2019], the graves found in both the north and south bays of Oikonomou Island would have been
constructed under the sea, whereas the rock-cut trenches on the coast of Voutakos and Kampos, would have been
mostly below sea level. If the sea level had been between -0.75 m and -1 m around 1000 AD [Evelpidou et al., 2014],
the flattened surface and the foundation of the Naoussa Castle would have been on an inundated area and the
threshing would have been carried out underwater on the Lageri coast.
In a recent publication, Bechor et al. [2019] suggested for the entire Cyclades plateau a Medieval sea level at 1.20 ± 0.26 m in 1300 ± 30 climbing to -0.70 ± 0.26 m in 1500 ± 30, based only on two measurements from the castle
of Naoussa (Paros). However, they did not take into consideration that (a) both constructions were founded on a
rocky outcrop with uneven elevations and with a sea level lower than its surface (Figure 13), and (b) the seawall and
the enclosure wall, which were built in different periods (13th-14th c. and 15th c., respectively), are today at the same
depth (-0.95 m and -1 m, respectively).

context_leads.title: New insights on the relative sea level changes during the Late Holocene along the coast of Paros Island and the northern Cyclades (Greece)
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
6. Late Holocene rsl changes in the northern and central Cyclades
Geomorphological, archaeological and historical evidence of past sea levels on the islands of Keos, Andros,
Kythnos, Syros and Paros, and the insular group of Mykonos, Rhenia and Delos, enabled us to determine six distinct
sea level stands in the northern and central Cyclades and draw the rsl curve for the last 6,300 years [Desruelles et
al., 2009; Mourtzas and Kolaiti, 2016; Mourtzas, 2018] (Figure 15b).
The Late Holocene history of the rsl changes begins with the sea level at 5.00 ± 0.10 m bmsl. Little evidence of
this earliest sea level is provided and is mainly limited to the deepest beachrock generation in the bays of Poles (SE
Keos, 5.15 ± 0.20 m bmsl), Kavia (Koundouros, SW Keos, 4.50 ± 0.20 m bmsl), Mesa Steno (S Andros, 4.97 m bmsl),

the coast of Paros (this study). According to Mourtzas [2012], this sea level stand probably lasted until 30 BC

this study]. This sea level stand has been established as being sometime between 30 BC (ancient Delos) and 41
AD (Palaeopolis, W Andros) and has been dated by the functional height of the Roman shipshed in Poises Bay
(W Keos), the submerged Roman structure in Exo Steno Gulf (S Andros), the Roman harbour of ancient
Palaeopolis (W Andros) [Mourtzas and Kolaiti, 1998; Mourtzas, 2010, 2012, 2018], the submerged Roman harbour

(Vlychadia, Agios Petros, Anerousa, Palaeopolis, Gyalia, Kremmydes, Mesa Steno bays, 1.30 m to 1.65 m bmsl),

context_leads.title: New insights on the relative sea level changes during the Late Holocene along the coast of Paros Island and the northern Cyclades (Greece)
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
7. The rsl curve for the northern and central Cyclades
The rsl curve for the northern and central Cyclades during the last 6,300 years is shown in Figure 15b. The
diagram collates the six successive periods of rsl stability for Paros and the relevant periods for the northern and
central Cyclades, their probable duration and the intervening periods of rsl change. Milestones such as important
events from the prehistory and history of the northern Cyclades (e.g. period of prosperity or abrupt abandonment
of a settlement), and significant geodynamic events, such as volcanic eruptions and strong earthquakes, that play
a key role in dating the former sea levels and their changes, are also indicated. The mean rsl curve represents the
mean rate of the rsl change during the Late Holocene for the northern and central Cyclades (Figure 15b).
The mean rate of rsl change, as deduced from the rsl curve for Paros and the northern and central Cyclades
(Figure 15b), increases from 0.63 mm/yr (3200-1050 BC) to 0.78 mm/yr (1050 BC-430 AD), 1.09 mm/yr (430-1390
AD), 1.54 mm/yr (1390-1780) and 2.35 mm/yr (1780 to date). It is noticeable that the rsl change rates are accelerating
and this is mainly attributed to glacio-istostacy, since the tectonic component is being redused over time. The mean
inferred rsl change rate of 0.96 mm/yr during the Late Holocene for the northern and central Cyclades is significantly
lower than that suggested by Lykousis [2009] at 1.38 mm/yr for the eastern Cyclades plateau for the time span
between ~425 ka BP and 13 ka BP.
The separation between tectonics and glacio-hydro-isostatic signals from the observed rsl curves allow us to
define the amount of tectonic contribution to the rsl change, and obtain the vertical tectonic rates [e.g. Lambeck,
1995; Lambeck et al., 2004; Antonioli et al., 2011; Anzidei et al., 2011, 2013, 2014]. Lambeck’s model [1996] predicts
a rising sea level for the Cyclades since 6,000 yr BP, which appears to be consistent with the observed rsl stand (I)
deduced from this study (Figure 15b). However, for the following observed rsl stands, a strong tectonic component
with respect to Lambeck’s (1996) prediction is extracted, ranging from 0.45 m to 1.06 m [sea level stand (II): 0.95
m, (III): 1.06 m, (IV): 0.84 m, (V): 0.62 m, (VI): 0.45 m]. The tectonic component that results from the model of Roy
and Peltier [2018] since 2 ka BP for the Cyclades is higher by 1 m than that of Lambeck [1996] for the same time span.

suggested by Stocchi et al. [2010], by comparing two different ice chronologies: ANU [Lambeck et al., 2004] and
ICE–5G [Peltier, 2004]. Although the seismic quiescence in the Cyclades archipelago, amid the intense seismic
activity of the Hellenic area [Jackson and McKenzie, 1984; Taymaz et al., 1991], projects the image of a
neotectonically inactive portion of the crust during the Late Holocene, the contribution of the tectonic component

stability, which signify long periods of tectonic quiescence and abrupt changes in the sea level, which are obviously
associated with strong deformation events. The “aseismically deformed” area of the northern and central Cyclades
is probably the result of the existence of a very closely spaced geometric fracture framework within the metamorphic
rocks, preventing strain accumulation. Thus, energy release manifests itself in continuous deformations creeping
along the fracture planes [Papanikolaou et al., 1981].

diagram collates the six successive periods of rsl stability for Paros and the relevant periods for the northern and
central Cyclades, their probable duration and the intervening periods of rsl change. Milestones such as important
events from the prehistory and history of the northern Cyclades (e.g. period of prosperity or abrupt abandonment
of a settlement), and significant geodynamic events, such as volcanic eruptions and strong earthquakes, that play
a key role in dating the former sea levels and their changes, are also indicated. The mean rsl curve represents the
mean rate of the rsl change during the Late Holocene for the northern and central Cyclades (Figure 15b).

(Figure 15b), increases from 0.63 mm/yr (3200-1050 BC) to 0.78 mm/yr (1050 BC-430 AD), 1.09 mm/yr (430-1390
AD), 1.54 mm/yr (1390-1780) and 2.35 mm/yr (1780 to date). It is noticeable that the rsl change rates are accelerating
and this is mainly attributed to glacio-istostacy, since the tectonic component is being redused over time. The mean

lower than that suggested by Lykousis [2009] at 1.38 mm/yr for the eastern Cyclades plateau for the time span

context_leads.title: New insights on the relative sea level changes during the Late Holocene along the coast of Paros Island and the northern Cyclades (Greece)
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
RSL change on Paros, N Cyclades
Aegean microplate. The correlation between the sea level stands determined for Paros and those for the northern and
central Cyclades revealed a uniform tectonic behaviour of the entire northern and central part of the Cyclades plateau.
The application of a geoarchaeological method of approaching the geomorphological and archaeological rsl
markers, including systematic observation, multiple and accurate measurements of depths/elevations and data
correction for tide and pressure effects, and also the deep understanding of the functionality of the ancient maritime
and coastal installations with respect to a past sea level, can enable us to determine and date the former sea level
stands, estimate the trends, magnitude and frequency of the vertical tectonic movements, and validate the proposed
geophysical models with greater accuracy.

context_leads.title: The so-called ‘Trade-Leagues’ in Early Greek History and the Lelantine War
context_leads.evidence_excerpt: Much has been written, in recent books and articles on early Greek history, of the so-called ‘trade-leagues,’ whose existence is thought to be implied by the statements of ancient writers about the feuds and alliances of the Greek cities before the Persian Wars. This conception is stimulating and in part sound, but over-simplified and ‘diagrammatic’; it is very easy, where the evidence is so incomplete, to make too much of such information as we have. The ‘trade-leagues’ did exist, but they must have been extremely loose-knit. Evidence of formal organisation such as we should naturally associate with the word ‘league’is wholly lacking. Miletus, Chios, Eretria and their allies—Samos, Chalcis, Corinth and their allies—form, each group, an entente cordiale rather than an alliance properly so called; and certain states, notably Naxos and Paros, seem to transfer their allegiance from one side to the other as circumstances dictate.

context_leads.title: Civic Identity and Sacred Memory at the Margins of Epic Geography: Paris/Alexandros, the Adrasteia Legacy and the Representational Repertoire at Parion
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
Abstract
This article examines Parion’s place within the epic and sacred geography of
the Troad through the relationship among civic identity, sacred memory and
public representation. It begins from the premise that the city’s identity
cannot be reduced to a single origin narrative, fixed etymology or
uninterrupted cultic continuity. Its central argument is that a distinctive
Parian repertoire of civic memory and representation can be reconstructed
from bodies of evidence belonging to different periods and carrying unequal
evidentiary weight. Colonisation and eponymic traditions, local sacred
genealogy, sacred topography, public commemoration and numismatic
imagery served different functions within this repertoire. Although Parion was
an Archaic foundation outside the Homeric narrative, its location between the
Propontis, Hellespont and Troad enabled later associations with the region’s
epic past. Strabo provides the principal textual basis for discussing Adrasteia,
Apollo Aktaios, Artemis, the reported transfer of sanctuary material and the
Altar of Hermokreon. Athenagoras’ contested Alexandros passage offers a
specific textual record of a taphos, bronze eikōn, sacrifice and festival in the
agora, while the Paris/Alexandros identification remains a defensible but nonexclusive modern reading. The Gorgoneion, Apollo Aktaios, Eros/Cupid and
Pario Conditori types document the circulation of selected images and sacred
or founding references without establishing collective belief, ritual continuity
or a single political programme. In the Roman period, local, sacred and epic
memories were rearticulated through colonial status and imperial visual
codes.
Keywords: Parion, Troad, sacred memory, Paris/Alexandros, numismatic
representation.

context_leads.context:
Abstract
This article examines Parion’s place within the epic and sacred geography of
the Troad through the relationship among civic identity, sacred memory and
public representation. It begins from the premise that the city’s identity
cannot be reduced to a single origin narrative, fixed etymology or
uninterrupted cultic continuity. Its central argument is that a distinctive
Parian repertoire of civic memory and representation can be reconstructed
from bodies of evidence belonging to different periods and carrying unequal
evidentiary weight. Colonisation and eponymic traditions, local sacred
genealogy, sacred topography, public commemoration and numismatic
imagery served different functions within this repertoire. Although Parion was
an Archaic foundation outside the Homeric narrative, its location between the
Propontis, Hellespont and Troad enabled later associations with the region’s
epic past. Strabo provides the principal textual basis for discussing Adrasteia,
Apollo Aktaios, Artemis, the reported transfer of sanctuary material and the
Altar of Hermokreon. Athenagoras’ contested Alexandros passage offers a
specific textual record of a taphos, bronze eikōn, sacrifice and festival in the
agora, while the Paris/Alexandros identification remains a defensible but nonexclusive modern reading. The Gorgoneion, Apollo Aktaios, Eros/Cupid and
Pario Conditori types document the circulation of selected images and sacred
or founding references without establishing collective belief, ritual continuity
or a single political programme. In the Roman period, local, sacred and epic
memories were rearticulated through colonial status and imperial visual
codes.
Keywords: Parion, Troad, sacred memory, Paris/Alexandros, numismatic
representation.

context_leads.title: Civic Identity and Sacred Memory at the Margins of Epic Geography: Paris/Alexandros, the Adrasteia Legacy and the Representational Repertoire at Parion
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
Genişletilmiş Özet
Parion, Propontis’in güney kıyısında, Troas ile Hellespontos arasındaki geçiş kuşağında yer alan bir kenttir. Bronz Çağı’na
bağlanan epik anlatının değil, sonraki kolonizasyon sürecinin ürünü olduğu için Homerosçu gelenekte bir odak olarak yer almaz;
ancak Troas’ın epik ve kutsal bellek alanlarına yakınlığı, bu mirasla daha geç dönemlerde ilişkilendirilmesine imkân vermiştir.
Çalışma, Parion kimliğinin tek bir köken anlatısına, sabit bir etimolojiye, kesintisiz kült aktarımına veya doğrudan bir Roma
siyasal programına indirgenemeyeceği yöntemsel öncülünden hareket eder. Merkezî savı, adlandırma, kutsal topografya,
kamusal anma, nümismatik temsil ve Roma koloni diline ilişkin farklı kanıtların Parion’a özgü bir kentsel bellek ve temsil
repertuarı içinde değerlendirilebileceğidir.
Makalenin yöntemi, farklı türdeki kanıtları aynı düzeye yerleştirmemeye dayanır. Antik tanıklıklar, geç mitografik anlatılar,
epigrafik ve nümismatik kayıtlar, modern topografik çalışmalar ve kuramsal literatür birbirini tamamlayan fakat aynı ağırlığa
sahip olmayan veri gruplarıdır. Strabon ve Athenagoras, makalenin iki temel antik tanıklık eksenini oluşturur; Frisch’in
testimonia derlemesi ise bu tanıklıkların izlenmesini sağlayan modern bir kontrol corpus’u olarak kullanılır. Bu ayrım sayesinde
antik kaynak, modern yorum, katalog verisi ve kuramsal çerçeve birbirinin yerine geçirilmez. Bu yöntem, bulgu ile yorumu
birbirinden ayırmayı da amaçlar.
Parion’un adlandırma ve yerel bellek gelenekleri, kolonizasyon bağlantıları, eponimik figürler, yerel kutsal soy ve Troas’ın
epik geçmişi arasında farklı ilişkiler kurar. Paros, Erythrai ve Miletos çevresindeki kolonizasyon gelenekleri, Parios/Iasion
eponimisi, Ophiogeneis’in yılan kökenli ve iyileştirici yerel soy belleği ve Paris/Priamos-Amandros anlatıları farklı kesinlik
düzeylerine sahiptir. Bu gelenekler tarihsel kuruluş belgeleri olarak değil, Parion’un koloni geçmişi, eponimik figür, yerel kutsal
soy ve Troas’ın epik belleğiyle ilişkilendirilmesini sağlayan farklı bellek unsurları olarak değerlendirilir.
Strabon’un Adrasteia, Apollon Aktaios, Artemis, kutsal alan malzemesinin Parion’a taşındığı yönündeki anlatı ve
Hermokreon Sunağı’na ilişkin aktarımı, Parion’un yakın kutsal topografyayla ilişkisini tartışmanın başlıca antik metinsel
dayanağıdır. Strabon daha eski ve günümüze ulaşmamış kaynaklardan yararlanmış olabilir; ancak bu pasajın kaynağı
belirlenememektedir. Pasaj, bildirilen malzeme transferi ile sunağın yeni anıtsal bağlamını tartışmaya imkân verir; kehanetin
sona erdiği bilgisi ise Adrasteia’daki ritüel işlevlerin Parion’da aynen sürdüğü yorumunu sınırlar. Ophiogeneis geleneği, Parion
çevresindeki yerel kutsal repertuarın yalnız Adrasteia-Apollon hattından ibaret olmadığını, yılan, iyileştirme, soy ve kutsal
topografya ilişkilerinin de kent belleğinde yer alabildiğini gösterir.
Athenagoras’ın Parion agorasına ilişkin tanıklığı, makalenin başlıca metinsel kayıtlarından biridir; ancak Alexandros’un
kimliği tartışmalıdır. Pasaj, agorada Alexandros’a ait bir taphos, bronz eikōn, kurban ve festival bilgisini doğrudan aktarır.
Schoedel’in Abonuteichuslu Alexandros yönündeki açıklaması ve Proteus/Peregrinus bağlamı dikkate alınırken, Corso ve KeleşYılmaz çizgisindeki Paris/Alexandros yorumu da modern literatürde savunulmuş bir okuma olarak değerlendirilir. Bu nedenle
pasaj, belirli bir yapının arkeolojik teşhisi veya tüm kurumsal yapısı belgelenmiş bir kahraman kültü olarak değil, agora içindeki
kamusal ve ritüel anmaya ilişkin özgül bir metinsel kayıt olarak kullanılır.
Gorgoneion ve boğa tipleri Parion’un erken kentsel tanınırlığını; Apollon Aktaios ve sunak betimleri Adrasteia ile
ilişkilendirilen kutsal referansların sikke dilindeki dolaşımını; Eros/Cupid tipleri sanat belleği ve yerel kült referanslarının Roma
dönemi görsel dili içinde yeniden ifade edilmesini; Pario Conditori tipi ise kurucu bellek, Parios/Parius-Paris muğlaklığı ve Roma
koloni dili arasındaki ilişkiyi belgeler. Parion’un yerel kentsel ve Roma dönemindeki koloni bağlamlarında üretilip dolaşıma
sokulan bu tipler, belirli imgeler ile kutsal veya kurucu referansların kamusal temsilini gösterir; ancak ortak inancı, ritüel
sürekliliğini veya tekil bir siyasal programı tek başlarına kanıtlamaz.
Roma dönemi, Parion kimliğini sıfırdan icat eden bir evre değil, yerel, kutsal ve epik bellek unsurlarının koloni dili ve
imparatorluk görsel kodları içinde yeniden dolaşıma girdiği tarihsel bağlamdır. Bu çerçevede Parion, epik anlatının dışında
kurulmuş bir kentte kutsal miras, yerel soy anlatıları, agora belleği, sanat ve kült referanslarının Roma dönemi temsil dili içinde
birlikte görünür olabildiği bir örnek sunar. Bu yönüyle makale, kentsel kimliğin geçmişe ilişkin unsurların mekân, anıt, ritüel ve
dolaşımdaki imgeler aracılığıyla yeniden düzenlenmesiyle şekillendiğini savunur.
Bu çerçevede makalenin katkısı, epik coğrafyanın sınırında kalan Parion’un farklı dönemlere ait bellek unsurlarının hangi
kanıt türleri aracılığıyla kamusal ve kentsel bir repertuar içinde anlam kazandığını açıklamaktır. Kolonizasyon gelenekleri, yerel
kutsal-soy anlatıları, Adrasteia ile ilişkilendirilen kutsal miras, agorada yoğunlaşan kamusal anma ve Roma dönemi sikke
imgeleri aynı tarihsel ağırlıkta değildir. Yazılı tanıklıklar, geç mitografik aktarımlar, topografik değerlendirmeler ve nümismatik
imgeler aynı tarihsel gerçekliğin doğrudan belgeleri olarak değil, Parion’un kentsel belleğini farklı düzeylerde izlemeyi sağlayan
kanıt grupları olarak kullanılır. Bu yaklaşım, kesinleştirilemeyen iddiaları sınırlandırırken kentin kimliğini mekânsal, ritüel ve
görsel pratikler üzerinden tartışılabilir kılar. Parion örneği böylece kentsel kimliğin farklı dönemlere ait bellek unsurlarının
mekân, anıt, ritüel ve dolaşımdaki imgeler içinde seçici biçimde yeniden bağlamlandırılmasıyla şekillendiğini ortaya koyar.

The article proceeds by this logic of evidence. The next section treats Parion’s naming, eponymic and
local sacred-genealogical traditions in the context of civic memory; the sections that follow discuss the
Adrasteia-Apollo Aktaios-Hermokreon axis, Athenagoras’ agora testimony, the numismatic data and the
Roman-period colonial language as different layers of evidence of the same model. This sequence avoids two
misleading alternatives: treating Parion as a rival epic centre to Ilion, or reducing it to a local colonial city.
Parion in Epic Geography: Naming Traditions and Civic Memory
Parion’s relationship with the epic geography of the Troad must be treated on a different plane from the
example of Ilion at the focus of the Iliad. Founded in the Archaic period, the city is not a natural part of the
epic narrative bound to the Bronze Age; its link with the memory of the Troad can therefore be discussed
not directly through a continuity of origin but through the layers of naming, descent, local sacred tradition
and epic association operating in later periods. The aim of this section is not to determine the ultimate
philological origin of the name Parion but to show what functions the relationships among the colonisation
traditions surrounding Paros/Erythrai/Miletos, the Parios/Iasion eponymy, the Ophiogeneis tradition and the
Paris/Priamos-Amandros narratives carried within civic memory.
The ancient traditions concerning the foundation of Parion do not converge around a single metropolis
narrative. Frisch records Erythrai, Thasos, Paros and a Miletos-Erythrai-Paros partnership in different forms,
while regarding the association with Paros as the more natural explanation (Frisch, 1983, pp. 59-60, no. T4347a). Keleş likewise notes Erythrai, Paros and Miletos, but stresses that the Miletos connection lacks
archaeological confirmation (Keleş, 2011, pp. 238-239). Özmen shows that modern scholars have interpreted
the roles of Paros, Erythrai, Miletos and Thasos differently (Özmen, 2024, p. 169). This plurality is better read
as a field of memory linking Parion’s past to different Aegean and Propontic connections. Malkin’s network
approach helps explain why such multiple origin narratives need not be treated as confused traditions, but
as relational ways in which poleis constructed the past (Malkin, 2011, pp. 8-9).
The second layer of naming memory is formed by the eponymous founder Parios or Parius. In the records
arranged by Frisch under T31-33, Parios/Parius explains the name Parion and is linked to the lineage of Iasion
(Frisch, 1983, p. 56, no. T31-33). These records are not documents of historical foundation, but eponymic
memory elements that bind the city’s name to a mythological genealogy. They do not identify Parios/Parius
with Paris/Alexandros; rather, they place him within the Iasion lineage. Curty’s work on legendary kinship
shows how mythological heroes or gods could provide cities with a language of relational past and legitimacy
rather than proof of historical origin (Curty, 1999, pp. 167, 184). In this sense the Parios/Iasion eponymy
functions as a memory mechanism linking Parion to a wider field of mythological descent and founder
figures.
Parion’s local sacred memory is not limited to the Parios/Iasion eponymy. Strabo’s immediately following
testimony reports that at Parion a genos called the Ophiogeneis claimed kinship with snakes and was
associated with a healing power against snakebites; the same record states that the arkhēgetēs of the genos
was recounted as a heros transformed from a snake (Strab. 13.1.14 = Frisch, 1983, p. 93, no. T107c). The
other attestations Frisch collects likewise show the Ophiogeneis as a local descent tradition around Parion to
which a snake origin and a healing power were attributed; the Aelianus tradition, for its part, transmits the
narrative of Halia’s union with a sacred snake in the grove of Artemis (Frisch, 1983, pp. 93-94, no. T107a-e).
This tradition is not directly connected with the Paris/Alexandros memory; but it points to a local memory
layer operating among the languages of descent, sacred power, healing and heros at Parion. The
Ophiogeneis thus shows that Parion’s repertoire of the past did not consist solely of colonial or epic
connections, and that local sacred-genealogical traditions too could hold a place within civic memory.
The Paris/Priamos-Amandros tradition, for its part, forms a later but striking layer in the association of
Parion with the epic geography of the Troad. In the late antique and Byzantine attestations Frisch collects
under T36-40, Priamos, on the prophecy that Paris would drive Troy to ruin, sends him to a distant territory
known by the name Amandra, Amandros or Mandro; in some variants he founds Parion there for Paris.
These narratives are not evidence of an early historical foundation; they are used here as late mythographic
transmissions preserved through Frisch’s arrangement of the Parion testimonia. The more secure
interpretation is to assess the Paris/Priamos-Amandros tradition as a mythographic transmission showing
that Parion could be associated with the Paris/Alexandros memory in the late antique and Byzantine periods

(Frisch, 1983, pp. 57-58, no. T36-40). The variants Amandra/Amandros/Mandro too are treated not as a
definite former name of Parion but as a toponymic tradition that locates the Paris narrative in the environs
of Parion.
At this point the interpretative value and the etymological evidential value of the phonetic proximity
among the names Parion, Parios, Paros and Paris are kept distinct from one another. The phonetic proximity
may have created a ground favourable for ancient and late antique authors to construct mythological
connections; but on its own it does not show that the name Parion derives from Paris. This proximity is, by
contrast, important for understanding why Parion’s naming memory could be associated with different
founder figures, genealogical narratives and epic connections. Instead of the proposition “the name Parion
comes from Paris”, it can therefore be said that the figure Paris/Alexandros is an epic element incorporated
into Parion’s later naming memory and civic-identity discourse.
The Roman-period Pario Conditori type shows that this memory of naming and founder figure continued
in the subsequent field of numismatic representation. Frisch’s record T34 transmits a youthful male head
and the legend Pario condit(ori) among the Parion attestations (Frisch, 1983, p. 56, no. T34). Since, however,
the catalogue, legend and iconographic variants of this type require numismatic verification, the detailed
assessment is taken up in the fifth section. What matters here is to note that the Parius/Paris ambiguity is
not entirely closed in the Roman-period visual idiom either, and that it adds a new visual dimension to the
discussion of foundational memory. In this section the Pario Conditori type functions not for iconographic
identification but as a bridge showing that the eponymic and epic naming memory could intersect with the
Roman colonial idiom; the consequences for interpretation that follow from defining the figure as Paris or as
Parius are taken up in the fifth section, within the framework of the problem of numismatic representation
and foundational memory.
Parion’s naming and local memory traditions therefore operate on four planes: colonisation narratives
connect the city to Aegean and Propontic networks; the Parios/Iasion eponymy frames the name through
founder-genealogy; the Ophiogeneis tradition adds a local sacred-genealogical layer; and the Paris/PriamosAmandros narrative attaches Parion to the epic memory of the Troad in later transmission. Athenagoras’
account offers a more specific textual record of public commemoration by referring to a taphos, bronze
eikōn, sacrifice and festival for Alexandros in the agora (Ath. Leg. 26.3-5 = Frisch, 1983, p. 58, no. T41).
Together, these strands outline Parion’s differentiated memory repertoire and prepare the discussion of the
Adrasteia-Apollo Aktaios-Hermokreon axis.
From Adrasteia to Parion: Apollo Aktaios, the Altar of Hermokreon and the Sacred Landscape
Parion’s relationship with the epic and sacred geography of the Troad cannot be explained solely through
naming traditions or the Paris/Alexandros memory. Adrasteia, in the city’s nearby sacred environment,
emerges through Strabo’s testimony as an important religious and spatial focus associated with Apollo
Aktaios, Artemis and an oracle within the wider Propontic cultic context surveyed by Erpehlivan (2019, pp.
39-40). In this section the term “sacred landscape” is used not in the sense of a broad landscape theory but
in the sense of a limited field of relations traceable among Adrasteia, Priapos and Parion through ancient
attestations and modern localisation proposals (Fig. 1). This usage is consistent with the polis literature that
stresses that sanctuaries could function not only as places of ritual practice but also as foci related to
communal belonging, the perception of space and territorial order. De Polignac’s approach to the function of
sanctuaries in ordering space and enabling the community to recognise itself within a particular territorial
framework provides a limited theoretical support for assessing the Adrasteia legacy to the extent that
Strabo’s testimony permits (de Polignac, 1995, pp. 19-20). This framework is not used as a substitute for the
ancient evidence; it only helps to explain why the Adrasteia material could become meaningful at Parion in
terms of civic memory.

unidentified, but the source of this passage cannot be established. Strabo reports that Adrasteia lay between
Priapos and Parion and that below it there was a plain of the same name. In the same passage he speaks of
an oracle of Apollo Aktaios and Artemis in this plain; he then relates that, upon the destruction of the

context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
monument (Keleş, 2018, pp. 24-25). Coins with altar depictions should therefore be used not for a definite
architectural restitution of the Altar of Hermokreon but to show that the sacred and monumental memory
connected with Adrasteia could be reflected in Parion’s coinage repertoire.
In the Roman period the Eros/Cupid types represent a different field of memory in Parion’s coin
repertoire. Frisch groups the Parion Eros tradition under T105, bringing together the ancient literary
testimonia and the relevant numismatic evidence; in the same context, on a coin of Commodus based on the
record in SNG Deutschland/Sammlung von Aulock, he transmits that on the reverse a large winged nude Eros
is depicted together with a small Herme and that the legend is Deo Cupidini (Frisch, 1983, p. 92, no. T105c).
Since this detail requires independent catalogue verification, it is used here only in respect of the presence
of the Eros/Cupid image in Parion’s Roman-period numismatic language. Keleş and Yılmaz likewise discuss
the Praxitelean Eros tradition at Parion through ancient literary testimony and pseudo-autonomous coins;
they note that on these coins the Deo Cupidini legend rearticulates Eros’ artistic and sacred position in civic
memory within the Roman-period visual language (Keleş & Yılmaz, 2021, pp. 383-384).
Kızılyalçın Oyarçin’s study of the Roman provincial coins found in the Parion excavations offers a limited
but important example of this tradition among the excavation finds. On the single Eros-depicting example,
dating to the reign of Severus Alexander, there is on the obverse a laureate bust of the emperor with
gorgoneion armour, and on the reverse a standing, winged Eros, a Herme at the lower left, and the legend
DEO CVPIDINI C G I A PAR (Kızılyalçın Oyarçin, 2023, pp. 205-206, Cat. No. 241, Pl. No. 25/241; Fig. 3a–b).
These types are not direct evidence of a Paris/Alexandros cult; they show rather the relationship Parion
constructed among its artistic prestige, its local Eros memory and the Roman-period visual language. It can
be taken into account that the Cupid figure had wide associations in the Roman world with the genealogical
narrative of Venus and Aeneas; but the Deo Cupidini type at Parion should not be read as a local reflection of
the Julio-Claudian dynasty or of an Augustan-period propaganda programme. The firmer interpretation is
that Parion placed its own Eros tradition back into circulation within the Roman-period coinage repertoire.
The Pario Conditori type is the numismatic problem that requires the most careful treatment in the
section. Frisch’s record T34 transmits, on the basis of BMC Mysia no. 83, a youthful male head and the
legend Pario condit(ori) among Parion’s founder-figure attestations (Frisch, 1983, p. 56, no. T34). A Parion
excavation specimen provides a related obverse, with a left-facing youthful male head and the legend PARIO
CONDIT, paired with a reverse showing the she-wolf and twins (Kızılyalçın Oyarçin, 2023, p. 325, Cat. No.
102, Pl. No. 11/102; Fig. 3c–d). This record is important because it suggests that the Parios/Parius and
Paris/Alexandros associations were not entirely closed in the Roman-period public visual field. Nevertheless,
the present source verification is not sufficient to fix the figure definitively as Paris or as Parius. For this
reason the type can be assessed less as a claim of iconographic identification than in respect of the
relationship between foundational memory and the Roman colonial language. The Parios/Iasion tradition
opens onto local eponymic founder memory, the Paris/Alexandros association onto the epic memory of the
Troad, and the conditor language onto Roman-period founder and colonial discourse. This flexibility shows
that Parion could place its founder-figure memory into circulation among different fields of meaning without
reducing it to a single identity.
At this point the interpretative consequence of the iconographic identification is important: if the figure is
read as Paris, the type makes Parion’s late mythographic Paris/Alexandros memory visible within Romanperiod language of foundation figures; if it is read as Parius/Parios, it points instead to the re-expression of a
local eponymous foundation tradition through colonial coinage. Since the present catalogue and publication
evidence is not sufficient to identify the figure securely with either option, the type is better understood as a
representational field in which foundational memory remained open to more than one reading within
Roman colonial titulature.
Taken together, Parion’s numismatic repertoire is significant less as a series of isolated documents than
as a set of visual choices made in different periods. The Gorgoneion and bull types gave the city an early and
recognisable civic image; the Apollo Aktaios and altar types brought Adrasteia-related sacred references into
the coinage repertoire; the Eros/Cupid types rearticulated local artistic and cultic memory in a Roman visual
idiom; and the Pario Conditori type kept foundation memory open between the Parios/Parius-Paris
ambiguity and Roman colonial vocabulary. Through coinage, Parion gave durable and circulating form to

Kızılyalçın Oyarçin, of the 355 Roman provincial coins found at Parion between 2005 and 2020, 273 are
Parion-minted; within the pseudo-autonomous group, of 43 coins 32 are Parion-minted, 24 of which date to
the period of Julius Caesar (Kızılyalçın Oyarçin, 2023, pp. IV-V, 177-178). The same study notes that the
reverse repertoire of the Parion-minted coins includes types associated with the Roman colonial titulature,
such as the she-wolf (Lupa), Romulus and Remus, the Genius, the priest/colonist and the plough (Kızılyalçın
Oyarçin, 2023, p. 177). These data show that in the Roman period Parion could strongly foreground its own
name and colonial status through coin circulation; but on their own they do not prove the implementation of
a specific centrally directed imperial programme. In this context the Pario Conditori type is important in
showing the intersection between local foundational memory and the Roman colonial language. As noted in
the fifth section, this type does not permit fixing the figure definitively as Parius or as Paris; its real
importance is that the conditor language made founder-figure memory legible within the representational
logic of the Roman period. The type thus shows, less than proving a single identity, that Parion could keep
foundation memory in play among the local eponymous tradition, the epic association of the Troad and
Roman colonial discourse.
The relationship between the Paris/Alexandros memory and Rome’s Aeneas-centred Trojan ideology
must also be assessed within this measured framework. Aeneas holds a special place for Rome as founding

context_leads.title: Civic Identity and Sacred Memory at the Margins of Epic Geography: Paris/Alexandros, the Adrasteia Legacy and the Representational Repertoire at Parion
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
altar, Eros/Cupid and Pario Conditori types brings together in the same visual field different references, from
Parion’s early civic recognisability to the sacred references connected with Adrasteia, to artistic memory and
to the Roman colonial language. These types do not on their own represent ritual practice or an integral
political programme; but they are important in showing which figures, images and sacred-founding
references Parion could carry into public representation.
The Roman period did not create this field of identity ex nihilo; rather, it provided a new representational
ground on which local, sacred and epic memory elements could be re-expressed through colonial status,
Latin legends and imperial visual codes. For this reason, Parion did not occupy the central position held by
Ilion in Rome’s relationship with the Trojan past; this, however, does not diminish the city’s importance.
Parion’s distinctiveness lies in the ability of a city remaining outside the epic centre of the Troad to relate,
within the same field of civic memory, its immediate sacred heritage, its local genealogical narratives, its
agora memory, its art and cult references, and the Roman-period colonial language.
The value of the Parion case lies in bringing uneven bodies of evidence into a single analytical frame
without flattening their differences. Ancient testimony, late mythographic transmission, local sacred
genealogy, monumental memory and coin imagery operate at different levels. Within that frame, selected
elements of Parion’s past became usable through names, genealogies, sacred heritage, public space,
monuments and circulating images. The case therefore supports a limited but methodologically important
conclusion: Parion’s civic identity took shape through the selective and recontextualised combination of
memory elements belonging to different periods and supported by evidence of unequal weight.

context_leads.title: Κέντρο Ναυτικού Πολιτισμού στην Πάρο Nautical Culture Center in Paros
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
Αντικείμενο της διπλωματικής εργασίας είναι ο σχεδιασμός ενός Ναυτικού Μουσείου στην Πάρο. Η άμεση συσχέτισή του με ένα υφιστάμενο καρνάγιο σκαφών, καθώς και η από κοινού προγραμματικές δραστηριότητες των δύο, καθιστούν την περιοχή παρέμβασης ένα νέο πόλο έλξης. Ένα ενιαίο Κέντρο Ναυτικού Πολιτισμού με κεντροβαρική σημασία στην πολιτιστική ζωή του νησιού και την εναλλακτική τουριστική του ανάπτυξη.
 Η προσέγγιση του θέματος έγινε αρχικά μακροσκοπικά, έχοντας ως απώτερο σκοπό την εξέταση μιας πιλοτικής εφαρμογής ομοίων παρεμβάσεων και σε άλλα νησιά των Κυκλάδων καθώς και τη λειτουργική επικοινωνία μεταξύ τους. Η  προτεινόμενη παρέμβαση επιθυμεί να προάγει ένα δυναμικό δίκτυο εναλλακτικού τουρισμού που σέβεται το πολιτιστικό κεφάλαιο των νησιών και διατηρεί την παραδοσιακή ναυτοσύνη στη ζωή των νησιωτών και στην αντίληψη των επισκεπτών, σε ένα σύγχρονο πλαίσιο.
 Η επιλογή της Πάρου ως τόπου παρέμβασης προέρχεται τόσο από το γεγονός ότι βρίσκεται ανάμεσα στα 3 πρώτα Κυκλαδονήσια που υφίστανται τη μεγαλύτερη τουριστική πίεση  όσο και από μία βαθιά γνώση και συναισθηματική σύνδεση με τον τόπο. Η Πάρος διαθέτει πλούσια ιστορία, παράδοση, φυσικό και πολιτιστικό πλούτο, όπως  και σημαντική τουριστική υποδομή. Το δομημένο περιβάλλον πυκνώνει στην παράκτια ζώνη παραλείποντας, ωστόσο, σημαντικές πολιτιστικές υποδομές, που μπορούν να αναδείξουν τις σημαντικές ιστορικές παραδόσεις του νησιού.
 Κύριο μέλημα της πρότασης του Ναυτικού Μουσείου είναι να συμβάλει στη διαφύλαξη και την προώθηση της ξυλοναυπηγικής τέχνης στο νησί, αναδεικνύοντας την πλούσια ναυτική του παράδοση και τη διαχρονική σημασία της ακτογραμμής του.

context_leads.title: Κέντρο Ναυτικού Πολιτισμού στην Πάρο Nautical Culture Center in Paros
context_leads.evidence_excerpt:
The subject of this diploma thesis is the design of a Nautical Museum in Paros island. The straight correlation of the museum with an existing traditional shipyard and the commonly organized activities of these two, create a strong point of interest for the whole region. Hence, the whole intervention is conceived as a Nautical Culture Centre with a significant value for the cultural side of the island and its alternative touristic development.
The approach to the subject was at first macroscopic, aiming to investigate possible similar interventions to the rest of Cyclades islands in a functional and strategical concept. The proposal’s main goal is to promote a dynamic and alternative touristic network with respect to the cultural load of Cyclades islands. There is an effort to preserve the traditional nautical culture and values in the life of the inhabitants and in the perception of the tourists, through a contemporary frame.
The selection of Paros as intervention site derives from a profound knowledge and emotional bond with the island, as well as from the fact that it is rated among the first 3 islands in Cyclades who face the biggest touristic pressure. Paros has long history, rich traditions, natural and cultural riches and important touristic infrastructure. Nevertheless, the built environment is becoming more dense along the coastline, missing out fundamental cultural infrastructure that could highlight the unique traditions of the island.
In this thesis, the proposal of the Nautical Museum aims to contribute to the safeguarding of the traditional boat craftsmanship in the island and the promotion of the timeless importance of its nautical culture and its coastline.

catalogue_leads.context_excerpt: λικία στο ριζικό κόμβο όσο και η διάμετρος στη βάση του ριζικού κόμβου των φυτών αναγέννησης βρέθηκαν να σχετίζονται με μορφολογικά χαρακτηριστικά και χαρακτηριστικά αύξησης των φυτών της πρόδρομης αναγέννησης των ειδών Q. frainetto και Q. petraea που εμφανίζονται κάτω από την κλειστή κομοστέγη της δρυός. Οι ηλικίες των φυτών της πρόδρομης αναγέννησης των δύο ειδών στις περιοχές Α, Β, Γ, Δ συνολικά, βρέθηκε να μην διαφέρουν σημαντικά. Στο είδος Q. frainetto οι μέγιστες ηλικίες (του ριζικού κόμβου) των φυτών της πρόδρομης αναγέννησης φτάνουν τα 10 – 12 έτη, ενώ στο είδος Q. petraea φτάνουν τα 12 – 1

catalogue_leads.context_excerpt: Mn-skarn ore deposits are relatively infrequent worldwide. A typical example of a Mn-skarn in the Attico-Cycladic Metallogenetic Massif is located at the mining area of Thapsana, Paros Island. The skarn occurs adjusted to the Thapsana biotite-garnet-tourmaline-lepidolite, highly sericitized, leucogranite apophyses of the Paros granitoid and related pegmatites and aplites dated from 11.5 to 7.5 Ma. The Mn-skarns orebodies occur as lenses and NE-trending veins hosted in the Cyclade

AB - Bhutan’s mask dance drama, Cham is performed in the festival of Tshechu. Originating from the 17th century, Tschechu is a religious ritual as well as a traditional festival held to commemorate the birth of Padmasambhava, who spread Buddhism in the kingdom of Bhutan. Bhutanese Cham and Tibetan Cham share similar traits in their content of , , and in their characters of Pawo and Pamo. Meanwhile, , , , , , , , are distinctive performances of Bhutanese cham. Moreover, the clown character Atsara in Bhutanese cham is a character that does not appear in the Tibetan Cham. Atsara, a humorous character, can be identified by its use of a long phallus ornament on the head or by a distorted face mask with a phallus in its hand. Bhutanese Cham, originally from Tibet, is a religious mask dance drama handed down in Lamaism temples. In later generations, new performances reflective of Bhutan’s history, myth, legends, and religion were added in large amount. Thus, the Cham of Bhutan now has very independent and characteristic aspects.
KW - Butan, Lamaism, Cham, Tshechu, Padmasambhava, Atsara

findings.title: 8 Recent archaeological work in the Cyclades (Geometric to Hellenistic)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The last decade marked a fruitful period for the archaeology of the Cyclades. The initiation and continuation of excavations,
surveys, and archaeological projects on a number of the islands, initiated by the Ephorate of Antiquities of the Cyclades of
the Hellenic Ministry of Culture, the foreign schools (EfA, AAIA, NIA), and Greek universities (University of Athens and of
Thessaly) offered new valuable evidence for the Cycladic history from the Early Iron Age to the Hellenistic era. New data
for the Early Iron Age have emerged on Andros (Zagora), Kythnos, and Despotiko. Excavations enlightened the form and components of the poleis during the Classical and Hellenistic periods (Palaiopolis, Vryokastro), revealed parts of cemeteries (Tenos,
Seriphos, Paros, Naxos), and enriched our knowledge on island cultic life from the Geometric period onwards (Vryokastraki,
Siphnos, Despotiko). The underwater surveys and excavations (Kythnos, Delos, Naxos) form one of the most interesting aspects of
recent archaeological work in the Cyclades, elucidating the maritime landscape and the operating trading networks.

findings.title: 8 Recent archaeological work in the Cyclades (Geometric to Hellenistic)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The rescue excavations running at the site of Kouphi, at the northeastern part of the island, since 2009
brought to light four underground chambers as well as a rectangular, three-roomed edifice on top
(ID5859). The destruction layer contained mainly pottery sherds of the sixth and fifth centuries BC. The
excavation of the underground chambers revealed a large amount of mostly storage, cooking, and transport
shapes, including numerous sherds of pithoi bearing relief decoration, dating from the seventh to the fourth
centuries BC. The function of these structures remains unknown (Pantou 2009b; 2014b: 2007–14).
The Roman theatre in the ancient polis of Melos has been inserted into a programme of anastylosis,
which resulted in the reconstruction of the lower part of the koilon, the orchestra, and the façade of the
scene (2010–2015). The excavation of the scene revealed a succession of rooms covered by a vault in
the lower levels. After the abandonment of the theatre in the fourth century AD, its premises continued
to be used as residences or workshops until the end of the sixth/early seventh century AD.

Paros
